content: The global spread of the highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza virus in 2006 was considered a significant pandemic threat. Previous strains of H5N1 were genetically distinct from the current strain, making the global dissemination of this new strain unprecedented. The current H5N1 strain is a highly pathogenic avian influenza virus (HPAI) that mutates rapidly and has been identified in multiple bird species. It is both epizootic (affecting non-human populations in an epidemic manner) and panzootic (affecting animals of many species across wide geographic areas). Unless otherwise specified, references to H5N1 in this context pertain to the recent highly pathogenic strain. In the first two months of 2006, H5N1 spread to Africa and Europe via wild bird populations, potentially marking the beginning of its endemic presence in migratory bird populations across multiple continents. This development has permanently altered poultry farming practices. The spread of H5N1 to wild birds, zoo birds, and occasionally mammals (e.g., pet cats) has raised numerous unanswered questions about the best practices for mitigating the threat. Efforts must balance reducing the risk of human and animal deaths from the current non-pandemic strain with minimizing the chances of the virus mutating into a pandemic strain. The use of vaccines presents a dilemma: not using them may necessitate the culling of large numbers of farm and zoo birds, while using them could increase the likelihood of a pandemic. By April 2006, scientists concluded that containment efforts had failed due to the role of wild birds in transmitting the virus. Consequently, they emphasized the need for more comprehensive risk mitigation and management strategies. In June 2006, the World Health Organization (WHO) predicted an increase in human deaths from H5N1 during late 2006 or early 2007. Significant increases in bird deaths due to H5N1 were recorded in Cambodia, China, Laos, Nigeria, and Thailand in July and August 2006, with an unparalleled rate of fatalities in Indonesia. In September, Egypt and Sudan reported a resurgence of bird deaths, followed by Vietnam and South Korea in December. On January 5, 2006, a second Turkish child from the same family died of bird flu, marking the first human death from H5N1 outside China and Southeast Asia. By January 7, two more children in Turkey were hospitalized with bird flu symptoms, later confirmed as H5N1, bringing the total number of cases in Turkey to five, with two fatalities. Since the outbreak began in 2003, 76 people had died from H5N1. On January 8, three individuals in the Turkish capital were hospitalized with suspected H5N1. On January 10, a woman in Turkey was diagnosed with bird flu as the country struggled to contain the outbreak. China announced two additional deaths from bird flu before 2006 began, and Indonesia confirmed the death of a 29-year-old woman from suspected bird flu. In Nigeria, birds began dying in January, but it was not confirmed as an H5N1 outbreak until February. On January 16, a 15-year-old Indonesian girl died of bird flu, and on January 18, China and Turkey each confirmed another human death from H5N1. A 13-year-old boy in Indonesia, the brother of the girl who died on January 16, also succumbed to the virus. Donor nations pledged $1.85 billion to combat bird flu at an international conference in China. By January 21, the WHO confirmed that two Indonesian children had died of H5N1. On January 29, H5N1 was detected in dead birds in northern Cyprus, prompting the European Commission to freeze animal and animal product transfers from the north of the island. On February 4, Indonesia confirmed three new cases of H5N1, two of which were fatal. A dead swan in Bulgaria tested positive for the H5 strain, with further testing initiated to confirm if it was H5N1. Over 20 dead birds were found along the Danube and in lakes near the Black Sea. On February 6, Nigeria submitted a preliminary report to the World Organisation for Animal Health (OIE) regarding a massive bird die-off that began in January. By February 7, the OIE/FAO Reference Laboratory in Italy confirmed the presence of highly pathogenic H5N1 in Nigerian samples. Nigeria became the first African country to confirm an H5N1 outbreak, affecting a commercial chicken farm in Kaduna State. By February 9, four new farms in Nigeria were confirmed to have H5N1 outbreaks. Experts from South Africa, the United States, OIE, and WHO were sent to assist Nigeria. The virus was expected to spread further in Africa, creating a severe situation. Farmers in northern Nigeria rushed to sell dead chickens at reduced prices before government bans were enforced. On February 10, officials in Azerbaijan identified H5N1 in wild birds found dead in the Caspian Sea. By February 11, Italy confirmed H5N1 in wild swans in Sicily and other regions, with similar findings in Greece and Bulgaria. On February 12, Slovenia confirmed the H5 virus in a wild swan, with samples sent to the UK for further testing. By February 13, Bulgaria confirmed a second case of H5 in a swan near the Black Sea, with additional cases reported across the country. On February 14, Austria reported its first case of H5N1 in two dead swans near Graz. Following the discovery of suspected H5N1 in swans on the German island of Rügen, authorities in Germany and other EU countries mandated that all poultry be kept indoors. On February 15, Slovenia declared the entire country a high-risk zone for bird flu after confirming H5 in a dead swan. Hungary identified H5N1 in dead swans, while Iran reported cases in wild birds. By February 17, Slovenia confirmed H5N1, and Egypt detected its first cases in several locations. France reported a case of H5N1 in a duck near Lyon. Iraq confirmed its second human death from H5N1, involving the uncle of the country's first victim. On February 18, India planned a poultry cull after reporting its first H5N1 cases. By February 19, the first suspected human death from bird flu was reported in India. On February 20, Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina confirmed H5 in dead swans. A UK laboratory confirmed H5N1 in dead swans from Bulgaria. On February 21, Malaysia confirmed H5N1 in chickens, and Croatia confirmed its previous day's case. By February 23, Slovakia confirmed H5N1 in dead birds. On February 25, France reported its first infected farm, with 80% of over 11,000 birds dying from H5N1. On February 27, Niger confirmed H5N1 in ducks near the Nigerian border, and Switzerland identified H5 in a dead swan. Bosnia confirmed its first H5N1 case in wild swans, leading to the culling of thousands of birds. On February 28, Sweden confirmed H5 in dead birds, while Finland ruled out H5N1 in dead ducks and a crow. By March 1, Switzerland confirmed its first H5N1 case in a dead swan, with a second case reported on March 2. Greece confirmed three new H5N1 cases in swans, bringing its total to 19. On March 3, Sweden confirmed eight new H5 cases, and Azerbaijan reported its first H5N1 case in poultry. On March 4, H5N1 was found in a wild goose in Germany, marking the sixth federal state to report the disease. Austria's H5N1 cases rose to 29. On March 5, Poland reported its first H5N1 case in a wild swan.
